title: SRE documentation: SLOs, error budgets, capacity planning, reliability initiatives, incident review standards, operational tooling, and runbooks
author: Ari Chen
content:
Overview

This document consolidates Redwood Inference's SRE standards and operational guidance for: SLO definition and error budget handling; capacity planning and forecasting; reliability initiatives and improvement projects; incident review standards; operational tooling recommendations; and canonical runbooks for production services. It is the single source of truth for teams responsible for operating inference control plane, serving-runtime, Dedicated clusters, and customer-facing APIs.

Audience
- SREs and on-call engineers
- Service owners and platform engineers
- Product and program managers involved in reliability work

Goals
- Provide a consistent SLO & error budget model across services so rollouts and automated mitigations behave predictably.
- Ensure capacity planning aligns with customer SLAs and cost targets.
- Standardize incident review and retrospective practices to reduce repeat outages.
- Document runbooks that are actionable, tested, and discoverable from alerts.

1) SLOs and Error Budgets

Principles
- SLOs measure user-facing reliability, not internal uptime. Use latency, availability, and correctness SLOs as appropriate.
- Keep SLOs simple: one primary SLO per user-facing capability (e.g., generation API availability).
- Error budgets are the operational allowance for failure — use them to make trade-offs between velocity and caution.

Standard SLO template (apply per service/route/model):
- SLO name: <service> / <capability> / <region>
- Metric: e.g., successful-response-rate, p95-latency, p99-latency, embed-success-rate
- Objective: e.g., 99.9% availability (monthly), p95 < 300ms (region-us-west)
- Measurement window: 30 days rolling (default)
- Alerting thresholds: see alerts section below
- Owner: service owner + SRE rotation

Canonical SLO table (examples):
| Service | Capability | Metric | Objective (30d) | Rationale | Owner |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| Redwood API (text-gen) | request success | successful-response-rate | 99.9% | customer-facing, low tolerance for failures | api-team |
| Redwood API (text-gen) | latency p95 | request-latency-p95 | < 300ms | interactive UX target | api-team |
| Embeddings service | request success | successful-response-rate | 99.7% | batch/analytics tolerant | embeddings-team |
| Dedicated inference | tail latency p99 | request-latency-p99 | < 1200ms | GPU scheduling variability | infra-team |

Error budget policy
- Error budget = 1 - SLO objective over measurement window.
- Burn rate calculation: observed_errors / allowed_errors over the same window.
- Policy buckets and actions:
  - Normal (burn rate < 1): continue normal development.
  - Elevated (1 <= burn rate < 2): notify service owner and SRE lead; restrict risky rollouts; accelerate mitigation tasks.
  - Critical (burn rate >= 2): pause non-essential deploys for the service; require postmortem within 72 hours if not already open; schedule priority reliability work.
- Quarterly review: every service must present current SLOs and error budget history during the SRE reliability review.

2) Alerting and Escalation (short summary)

Alerting principles
- Alert on symptoms not causes (e.g., request-failure-rate high, p99 latency spike).
- Use composite alerts where needed to reduce noise.
- Route alerts to PagerDuty with clear runbook links and context fields (recent deploys, error budget state, recent alerts).

Standard alerts and thresholds (examples):
- P0 Availability: successful-response-rate < SLO objective for 5m -> P1 PagerDuty, immediate paging to on-call.
- P1 Latency: p99 > SLO threshold for 5m -> P1 PagerDuty.
- P2 Resource: worker-error-rate > 2% for 30m -> P2 notification to Slack channel + ticket.
- Error budget burn alert: burn rate >= 1.5 in 24h -> notify service owner + SRE lead.

Escalation flow
1. On-call acknowledges and triages within 5 minutes.
2. If not resolved in 15 minutes, escalate to secondary on-call and SRE lead.
3. If impact includes customer-visible outages or revenue impact, declare incident and follow incident response procedure.

3) Capacity Planning and Forecasting

Cadence and owners
- Monthly capacity review: infra-team + platform + product representatives.
- Quarterly demand forecasting sync with finance and sales for Dedicated and Private capacity commitments.

Inputs and signals
- Utilization metrics: GPU/CPU/Memory utilization, queue lengths, scheduler backlogs.
- Traffic signals: requests-per-second (RPS), average sequence length, token-per-request trends.
- Business signals: committed Dedicated capacity, upcoming launches or marketing events, model catalog additions.

Forecasting method (standard):
1. Baseline traffic growth = 90-day rolling average growth rate (daily granularity).
2. Adjust for known events: launches, enterprise commitments, region activation.
3. Convert RPS -> GPU-hours using historical per-model profiles (tokens/sec, batch size, effective throughput).
4. Add safety buffer: N weeks of headroom (default: 4 weeks) -> converts to % capacity reserve (default 20%).

Capacity playbook (high level):
- If utilization > 70% sustained for 48h, schedule urgent capacity increase or enable burst pools.
- If queue depth increases above configured threshold (service-specific), throttle non-critical throttled jobs and activate backpressure.
- Maintain a cross-region spare pool to handle regional failover (default: 10% of global serving capacity).

4) Reliability Initiatives and Roadmap Integration

Classifying initiatives
- Reactive: fixes tied to recent incidents (postmortem-derived).
- Proactive: capacity resilience, automated rollbacks, improved observability.
- Strategic: long-term platform changes (kernel improvements, KV cache architecture, quantization improvements).

Initiative lifecycle
1. Proposal with impact metrics (expected reduction in MTTR, error budget savings, cost delta).
2. SRE prioritization review (monthly).
3. Scoped implementation with test plan and rollout strategy.
4. Post-launch measurement vs. expected impact.

Example reliability project types
- Prefix/KV cache warm-up to reduce cold-start p99s.
- Autoscaling policy improvements to reduce manual intervention.
- Model-split routing to migrate traffic to lower-cost variants when error budget permits.

5) Incident Review Standards and Postmortems

When to run a postmortem
- Any incident that meets business-impact threshold: customer-visible downtime, SLA breach, or critical data loss.

Postmortem structure (required fields)
- Title and incident ID
- Severity and duration
- Summary (what happened, customer impact)
- Timeline of events (UTC timestamps, actions taken)
- Root cause analysis (5 Whys or causal graph)
- Contributing factors and systemic issues
- Corrective actions (owner, due date) and follow-up tasks
- Error budget impact and measurement
- Lessons learned and proposed reliability initiatives

Blamelessness and remediation
- Postmortems must be blameless and focused on system and process improvements.
- Each corrective action must be tracked in our task tracker with due dates and linked back to the postmortem.

6) Operational Tooling (recommended stack)

Monitoring and observability
- Metrics: Prometheus / Thanos for long-term metrics retention; standard exporters instrument services for: request rate, success rate, latency (p50/p95/p99), CPU/GPU utilization, queue depth, and cache hit rates.
- Tracing: OpenTelemetry -> Jaeger/Honeycomb for distributed traces and tail-latency analysis.
- Logs: structured logs to Loki or Elastic with standardized fields (request_id, model_id, route, region, owner).
- Dashboards: Grafana per-service SLO dashboard with error budget panel, alert history, and recent deploys.

Alerting and paging
- PagerDuty for on-call routing and escalation policies.
- Alerts must include runbook link, relevant Grafana panels, recent deploy commit, and error budget state.

Operational automation
- Canary deployment tooling integrated with CI (example: rollout if error budget available and canary success criteria met).
- Automated rollback criteria: 5m sustained error-rate > 2x baseline or critical alert fires.

Runbook management
- Runbooks are stored as Confluence pages and referenced in alert payloads.
- Each runbook must include: purpose, owner, detection criteria, immediate remediation steps, escalation contacts, and post-incident tasks.

7) Canonical SRE Runbooks (examples)

A) High error-rate on Redwood API (generation requests)
- Symptoms: success-rate drops below SLO for 5m OR p99 latency spikes > 2x SLO.
- Immediate steps (0-10m):
  1. Acknowledge alert and set incident channel (Slack #incident-<service> and create incident in pagerduty).
  2. Check Grafana SLO panel, recent deploys, and recent config changes (feature flags).
  3. If deployment occurred in last 30 minutes, roll back to last known good commit.
  4. If no deploy, identify spike source by model_id, route, and region using logs and traces; triage to dev owning model-serving or runtime.
- Mitigations (10-60m):
  - Shift traffic to fallback smaller model variant if rate-limited by kernel performance.
  - Increase autoscaler min replicas for critical path.
  - Enable temporary rate-limiting for noisy tenants.
- Recovery and follow-up (post-incident):
  - Run postmortem and create corrective actions.
  - Update SLO dashboard if metrics were mis-instrumented.

B) GPU node failure (Dedicated cluster)
- Symptoms: node marked NotReady, pods evicted, scheduling latency increases.
- Immediate steps:
  1. Acknowledge and set incident channel.
  2. Use kubectl and cloud provider console to check node condition and recent maintenance events.
  3. If hardware failure, drain node and promote capacity from burst pool; notify capacity planning.
- Mitigations:
  - Rebalance pods and evict less-critical workloads.
  - If contiguous node failures affect SLO, trigger cross-region failover.
- Recovery and follow-up:
  - Replace faulty hardware and validate kernel drivers and CUDA versions.
  - Automate detection rule to preemptively cordon nodes with early error signals.

C) Slow KV cache (serving runtime)
- Symptoms: cache hit rate drops, p99 generation latency increases for warm-start requests.
- Immediate steps:
  1. Confirm cache metrics (hit rate, eviction rate).
  2. Restart cache-workers if they show memory pressure or leaked sockets.
  3. Temporarily increase cache size on affected cluster to restore hit-rate.
- Mitigations:
  - Roll out cache tuning profile and warm-up scripts in the autoscale pipeline.

8) Runbook hygiene and testing

Requirements for every runbook
- Owner and secondary owner listed with pager duty escalation roles.
- Verification steps that can be executed by the on-call within 10 minutes.
- Runbooks must be reviewed at least once every 6 months and after any incident referencing them.

Testing runbooks
- Quarterly runbook drills: SRE drills replicate an incident scenario and validate runbook completeness.
- Game days: execute cross-team migration/playback scenarios (e.g., region failover, model rollback).

9) Metrics and KPIs for the SRE org

SRE health dashboard should include:
- Service-level SLO compliance (percentage of services meeting SLO)
- MTTR (median and 95th) per severity class
- Error budget burn rate distribution across services
- Time-to-detection and time-to-recovery metrics
- Number of reliability initiatives completed vs planned

10) Ownership and governance

- Each service must have an assigned service owner and at least one SRE lead responsible for SLOs and runbook accuracy.
- The SRE guild governs standards, triages cross-cutting reliability initiatives, and runs the monthly reliability review.
- Exceptions to SLO or capacity standards require approval from the SRE guild and documentation of compensating controls.

Appendices
A. Useful CLI snippets
- Check SLO panel via Grafana API: curl -u <user>:<token> https://grafana.internal/api/dashboards/uid/<uid>
- Prometheus query examples:
  - success_rate: 100 * (sum(rate(http_requests_total{code!~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total[5m])))
  - p99 latency: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le))

B. Templates
- Postmortem template link: /confluence/eng-sre/postmortem-template
- Runbook template link: /confluence/eng-sre/runbook-template

C. Contacts and escalation roster
- SRE lead on-call: sre-lead@redwood-inference.internal
- PagerDuty: Redwood-SRE schedule
- On-call rotation: listed in team wiki /confluence/eng-sre/oncall-rotation
